vehemently

/VEE-uh-muhnt-lee/ - the stress falls on VEE · adverb

Hear It

What It Means

Vehemently means marked by intense force or emotion.

The twins opposed selling the lake cottage vehemently, itemizing forty summers of reasons before the realtor had finished her coffee.

Example

The idea seemed harmless: brighten the chapel's faded fresco with a modern glaze. The restorer's answer was not harmless. She objected vehemently — voice low and shaking, a folder of pigment analyses laid out page by page, and her resignation, signed and dated, drawn from her bag in case the point was unclear. The fresco stayed faded.

Vehemently is the exact word because it names expression driven by intense force and feeling. She isn't merely firm — firm doesn't bring a resignation letter. The intensity is the information: whatever she is saying, the force with which she says it has become part of the message.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fiercely: Fiercely is intensity with open ferocity in it — teeth showing, an edge of attack in the voice or the eyes. Vehemently is intense feeling driving the words, and it can stay perfectly controlled, even quiet. A fierce denial snarls; a vehement one can be nearly whispered and still burn.

forcefully: Forcefully means with strength — weight and momentum behind the words — but not necessarily with feeling; a lawyer can argue forcefully about a clause she cares nothing for. Vehemently requires the feeling: the intensity comes from emotion, and the force is the heat escaping.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

mildly: with the heat turned all the way down

halfheartedly: with too little feeling to matter

Where it sits · how much hot feeling drives the words

insistently → vehemently → furiously

insistently vs. vehemently: Insistently keeps returning to the point and won't drop it; vehemently adds the force of real feeling to the asking.

furiously vs. vehemently: Furiously goes past vehemently — the force has become anger outright, and the argument is now a fight.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vehement: intense, forceful (Latin vehemens, origin debated)

Suffix — -ly: in the manner of

Put it together: Vehement (intense — Latin vehemens) + -ly (in the manner of): the root is a single Latin block, and even Rome argued about where it came from. What never changed is the meaning — force of feeling pushed into expression — and the -ly simply sets that force in motion.

A word even the Romans couldn't take apart: Latin vehemens may be from vehere, 'to carry' (carried away by feeling), or from ve- + mens, 'out of one's mind' — Roman grammarians themselves disagreed, and no other English word grew from either branch through this one. Some words arrive whole; this one arrived at full volume.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / forceful

Vehemently turns the intensity dial on a verb of speech or stance — deny, object, oppose, insist. The force is feeling, not volume: a vehement refusal can be nearly whispered, which is exactly where it parts company with this unit's vociferous, the word for loudness itself. If the feeling is everyday and only the grip is tight, firmly is the honest adverb.
